extracted.intended_audience: journalism students, copy readers, reporters, and newspaper desk editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and exercises for newspaper make-up, copy reading, grammar, punctuation, style, and correction marks aimed at preparing, editing, and setting newspaper copy and headlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisites for Copy Reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Thorough knowledge of news-writing principles is indispensable; copy readers must know how to write a good story themselves and have quick perception of news values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At least one semester of successful experience as a reporter is recommended for desk appointments. The copy reader must be alert for errors in grammar, rhetoric, spelling, punctuation, libelous/inaccurate statements, weak leads, buried features, repetitions, editorializing, wordiness, irrelevancy, and dullness. The copy reader shares responsibility with the reporter for accuracy, interest, and clearness.

rubrics_metrics.name: The 'Demons' of Grammar
rubrics_metrics.description: Four recurring grammatical problems that cause trouble at the copy desk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'demons' are: (1) disagreement of verbs and their subjects, (2) faulty reference of pronouns, (3) misplacement of modifiers, and (4) upside-down subordination. These should be given special attention by copy readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement of Verbs with Subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: A verb should agree in number with its subject, not with intervening words or predicate nouns; certain pronouns and indefinite words are singular; phrases joined by with, together with, including, etc., do not make subjects plural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of incorrect/correct usage are provided (e.g., 'A new compilation of facts and figures has been made.' not 'have been made'; 'Each of the men was arrested for his part in the plot.' not 'were arrested for their part'). Use singular verbs with words like each, every, either, neither, somebody, anyone, nobody, one, a person, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faulty Reference of Pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Every pronoun should refer unmistakably to a definite antecedent; avoid reference to a general idea, an implied word, or a subordinate word that creates doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sentences where the pronoun's antecedent is ambiguous. Examples: Wrong: 'He became very angry, which caused his death.' Right: 'He gave way to a fit of anger, which caused his death.' Recast sentences to make antecedents clear; rewrite indirect references into explicit constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misplacement of Modifiers (Dangling Modifiers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Participles, gerund phrases, and elliptical clauses must logically modify the subject they are nearest; adverbs like only and just should be placed next to the words they modify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and correct dangling participles/gerunds and misplaced adverbs. Examples supplied: Wrong: 'Becoming engrossed in the play, our appointment with you was forgotten.' Right: 'Becoming engrossed in the play we forgot our appointment with you.' For positioning of only/just: Wrong: 'I only finished two tasks.' Right: 'I finished only two tasks.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Upside-down Subordination
rubrics_metrics.description: The important idea in a sentence should be in the main clause, not the subordinate clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite sentences so the main clause contains the principal idea. Example: Wrong: 'He had just reached the corner, when suddenly his car got beyond control...' Right: 'Just as he reached the corner, his car got beyond control and crashed...' Also prioritize the main idea in sentence structure for clarity and emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of Wordiness / Use of Right Expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid cumbersome familiar phrases by eliminating unnecessary words; prefer concise constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provided list of wordy expressions with corrected forms (e.g., 'all the different' → 'all the'; 'appear to be' + 'to be' avoided: 'appear happy' not 'appear to be happy'; 'first of all' → 'first'; 'for the purpose of' → 'for'; 'nobody else but' → 'nobody but'; 'report to the effect that' → 'report that'; don't use 'a short space of time' → 'a short time'; remove redundant 'of all' or 'therefore' in certain constructions). Includes exercises to rewrite stories to remove unnecessary words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page Make-up and Heading Schedules (Schedules A, B, C)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan first-page make-up using specified heading sizes and story lengths (schedules define heading numbers and unit ranges for layouts of 5-, 6-, and 7-column papers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises present concrete materials (stories with inch lengths and heading categories) and require planning make-up for different column counts and schedules (A, B, C), adapting headings, dropping heads or stories as necessary, and arranging cuts. Guidance implies understanding proportions, visual balance, and hierarchy of headings when composing front pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style Sheet — Capitalization Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspaper capitalization differs from literary style; rules define what to capitalize and what not to capitalize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize all proper nouns, names of months/days (not seasons), principal words in titles (including initial A or The), titles of newspapers/magazines (but do not quote them), official titles when preceding a name, distinguishing parts of organization names, proper nouns in geographic names (with exceptions), abbreviations of degrees, distinguishing parts of holidays, names of races/nationalities (exceptions noted), nicknames of athletic clubs, names of notable events, particles in French/German/Spanish/Italian names when used without a personal name. Do not capitalize names of political parties, common bodies/offices (congress, senate), school studies except languages, titles when they follow the name, certain abbreviations/time notations, names of school classes, spelled-out college degrees, 'former' before a title, and specified nouns after proper nouns (street, avenue, etc.). Examples and numbered rules (1–28+) are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style Sheet — Quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for when to use quotation marks and how to format quotations in newspaper copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote all verbatim quotations when set in same type and measure as context; quote testimony, conversation, interviews in direct form except certain formatted Q&A; quote names of books, plays, paintings, etc.; use single quotes for quotations within quotations; use quotation marks at beginning of each paragraph in a long continuous quotation but only at the end of the last paragraph; do not quote familiar nicknames, names of characters in books/plays, or names of vessels/sleeping cars/race horses/dogs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style Sheet — Figures (Numbers)
rubrics_metrics.description: When to use figures versus spelling out numbers in newspaper style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use figures for numbers of 10 or greater. Use words for numbers less than 10 except in specified cases: hours of day (7 p.m.), days of month (September 3), ages (9 years old, 2-year-old), all dimensions/prices/percentages/dates/votes/calibers/times/stock quotes/scores, all sums of money (use $ and omit decimal .00 for whole dollars), street and room numbers, when used in close connection with numbers greater than 10, and other specified contexts. Guidance includes examples and exceptions for approximations ('about a hundred men').

rubrics_metrics.name: Style Sheet — Abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Which titles and words may be abbreviated and which should not in newspaper copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abbreviate only specified titles when they precede a name (Rev., Dr., Mr., Mrs., M., Mme., Mlle., Prof., and military titles with exceptions). Abbreviate names of states only when they follow city names. Use No. before figures for numbered items. Abbreviate 'Saint' and 'Mount' in proper names but not 'Fort' or 'Port'. Do not abbreviate railway/street/district/company unless the company does so, do not abbreviate Christian names, do not abbreviate titles like congressman/senator/president etc., do not abbreviate months except in dates and datelines, do not abbreviate years, and avoid Xmas for Christmas; use 'cents' spelled out except in market quotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dates and Datelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Formatting rules for dates and date lines in newspaper copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In running text use 'Sept. 27, 1922' not 'the twenty-seventh of September'. Punctuate date lines as 'Reardan, Wash., May 1 —' and omit the state name after prominent city names. Abbreviate months of more than five letters in datelines and omit the year after the month/day date in datelines. Begin the story immediately after the dash on the same line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles and Name Usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for giving initials/names and how to use titles for persons in first mentions and lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always give initials or first names the first time a person is mentioned. Never use only one initial; use both initials or the full first name. Do not use 'Mr.' with initials or first name; mention a man by initials or first name plus last name and thereafter Mr. + last name. For women, use Miss or Mrs. with first name or initials in first mention; always indicate unmarried women with Miss and married with Mrs.; give first names of unmarried women (not initials). Start lists of unmarried women with Misses and married with Mesdames; begin lists of men's names with Messrs. Supply 'the' before Rev.; supply 'Mr.' after the title if first name is omitted; write Mr. and Mrs. James Smith, not 'James Smith and wife'. Give 'Professor' only to persons of professional rank. Do not use 'Honorable' except in quotations/foreign matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation of Copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical rules for preparing copy for the compositor and the desk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write legibly and use a typewriter when possible. Never write on both sides of the paper. Double-space both typewritten and longhand copy. Use soft copy paper. Begin every story about one-third down the first page. Number sheets at the top and mark numbers with half circles. Put an end mark at the close of every complete story. In longhand copy print proper names and use underscoring/overscoring conventions for w's and n's/m's. Put the abbreviated story name and the writer's name at the upper left-hand corner of each sheet. Follow the style sheet consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation — General Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid punctuation that is not absolutely necessary; punctuation is for clarity, not ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspaper paragraphs are short and paragraph indentation functions like punctuation. Use only punctuation necessary to clarity. The text then details the specific uses for periods, semicolons, colons, commas, question marks, dashes, parentheses, and apostrophes with many examples and exceptions (see items 76–106 for rules and illustrative examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation — Specific Uses (Period, Semicolon, Colon, Comma, Question Mark, Dash, Parentheses, Apostrophe)
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed usage rules for each punctuation mark in newspaper style, including when to use semicolons between clauses, colon for lists/quotations/times, comma uses (appositives, absolute phrases, dependent clauses, series), question mark for direct questions and questionable data, dash for broken sentences/parenthetical material/summaries, parentheses for long parenthetic expressions and editorial insertions, apostrophe rules for omission and possessives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Use semicolon to separate series members that contain commas; use colon after a phrase introducing a list or long quotation; use comma to set off appositives and nonrestrictive modifiers; use question mark after direct questions and to indicate doubtful dates; dash when a sentence is broken off or to set off long parenthetical expressions; use parentheses to enclose explanatory words and editorial notes within quotations; apostrophe to indicate omitted letters and to form possessive singular ('John's book'), with guidance on 'it's' vs 'its' and forming plurals of letters/numbers. Numerous illustrative examples are provided in the chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word Combinations, Compounds, and Hyphenation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for writing compound adjectives, common nouns used adjectively, prefixes, suffixes, and which compounds are written solid, separate, or hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compound adjectives/common nouns used adjectively generally take a hyphen (first-class man). Adverbs ending in -ly with participles do not take a hyphen (newly built). Prefixes self-, ante-, post-, semi-, anti- take hyphen; many prefixes (re-, non-, over-, under-, sub-, inter-, trans-) form single words (interstate). Suffix 'like' forms one word (childlike). Lists of many words written solid (e.g., airship, newspaper man? — note exceptions), lists of combinations written separate (e.g., any one, a while, back yard), and lists requiring hyphen (e.g., anti-trust, brother-in-law, 6-year-old child) are provided to guide usage and spelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks Used in Correcting Copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventions for marking corrections on copy to indicate deletions, transpositions, spelling/numeral format changes, paragraph starts, and other editing instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strike through words or lines to delete (do not enclose in parentheses or erase). Circle numbers to indicate spelling out or conversion to figures. Indicate transpositions clearly with marks. Mark the beginning of every paragraph. Separate run-together words with a diagonal. Place an end mark at the conclusion of every story so compositor knows nothing is to be added. In longhand: print all names, underscore w's and overscore n's and m's; to indicate that text struck out should stand, place a row of dots under them and mark 'stet' in the margin. Write 'folo copy' to indicate copy should be set as written despite errors.
